The Nandus nandus, commonly known as the Gangetic leaffish, exhibits life-history traits that reflect its adaptation to the lentic and slow-flowing freshwater systems of South Asia. Upon hatching, prolarvae measure just a few millimeters, with the wet weight at birth being an exceedingly modest 0.000165 grams [Wwb = 0.000165 grams], a value derived from an egg diameter of approximately 0.68 millimeters. Embryonic development proceeds rapidly at the elevated temperatures characteristic of its tropical nursery habitats; laboratory-reared cohorts maintained at a constant 28 °C [T = 28 °C] display a brief incubation period of roughly 3 days [ab = roughly 3 days] before the yolk-sac larva emerges. This lecithotrophic stage relies entirely on endogenous reserves, and the timing of chorion rupture is tightly coupled to the thermal regime. The small birth mass places Nandus nandus among the more diminutive freshwater teleosts at emergence, a trait that likely imposes strong selective pressures on early feeding success and predator avoidance during the vulnerable larval period.

Puberty in the Gangetic leaffish is attained at a relatively modest body size, marking the transition to the reproductively active adult phase. Field studies have established that individuals become capable of reproducing once they reach a total length at puberty of 9.1 centimeters [Lp = 9.1 centimeters]. This somatic milestone is also associated with a corresponding wet weight at puberty of 9.5 grams [Wwp = 9.5 grams], a value that reflects the energetic investment needed for initial gamete production. The weight-length relationship follows a power function typical of ambassid fishes, with the puberty weight derived from the length measurement. Reaching this size threshold generally requires several months of growth in productive floodplain habitats, though variation in resource availability can shift the timing considerably. The onset of gonadal recrudescence, marked by vitellogenesis in females and spermiation in males, signals that the physiological machinery for reproduction has been activated, preparing the individual for its first spawning event in the coming monsoon season.

The species attains its maximum body dimensions after a period of sustained post-pubertal growth, with the ultimate total length recorded at 20 centimeters [Li = 20 centimeters] for the largest individuals encountered in natural populations. This corresponding ultimate wet weight of 102.8 grams [Wwi = 102.8 grams] represents the asymptotic body mass, beyond which further somatic expansion becomes negligible. This weight was estimated from the length-weight relationship applied to the maximum recorded length. In comparison to other members of the Nandidae family, the Gangetic leaffish occupies an intermediate position in terms of maximum size, being substantially larger than the dwarf forms but far smaller than the African and South American leaf fishes. The progression from the juvenile stage to this maximum size is characterized by gradual allometric shifts, with the deepening of the compressed body form that defines the species' distinctive leaflike silhouette, an adaptation that facilitates ambush predation among submerged vegetation.

Longevity records for Nandus nandus, drawn from captive-rearing studies, indicate that individuals maintained at a stable 28 °C [T = 28 °C] may survive for up to 3 years [am = up to 3 years], a lifespan that spans approximately 1,095 days under these controlled thermal conditions. This duration is consistent with the semelparous or weakly iteroparous reproductive strategy observed in many small-bodied tropical freshwater fishes, where high adult mortality in unpredictable monsoon environments favors early and concentrated reproductive effort. Natural mortality in the wild is likely higher, driven by predation from piscivorous birds and larger fish, as well as habitat desiccation during dry-season drawdowns. Senescence typically manifests as a decline in body condition and a loss of spawning vigor during the third year, with physiological deterioration accelerating once the reproductive peak has passed. The relatively compressed lifespan places the species on the faster end of the life-history continuum within its guild, a pattern reinforced by the early age at maturity.

Reproductive output in the Gangetic leaffish is partitioned across the breeding season, with mature females depositing multiple clutches annually. During a single spawning event, a gravid female typically releases between 200 and 400 eggs per spawning event [N_R_i = between 200 and 400 eggs per spawning event], each measuring roughly 0.68 millimeters in diameter, which are adhesive and attach to submerged aquatic vegetation. The number of spawning events per year is estimated at 3 clutches per year [F_R_i = 3 clutches per year], a frequency that aligns with the multiple monsoon pulses that trigger gonadal recrudescence. This reproductive strategy, combining a moderately large clutch size with repeated spawning activity, yields a considerable annual fecundity that compensates for the high egg and larval mortality inherent in the species' floodplain nursery habitats. The adhesive eggs are guarded by the male in natural nests, a parental behavior that improves survival rates through the early developmental stages. The spawning season is synchronized with the summer monsoon, ensuring that newly hatched larvae encounter abundant zooplankton prey as they begin exogenous feeding following yolk-sac resorption.
